Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00467

The Active Intellect acts on the soul and its images as the sun acts on a healthy eye and on the things before it. Before the sun rises, the eye can see only in potential, and the things around it can be seen only in potential. When sunlight reaches the eye, the eye actually sees and the things before it become visible. In the same way, when this sacred light reaches the soul and its imagined ideas, the soul becomes an actual intellect, able to think, and its imagined ideas become actual objects of thought. The intellect then distinguishes what is essential from what is accidental, what is real from what merely accompanies it, and what is basic from what follows from it. It understands these things apart from their numbers and individual instances. The human being then becomes an intellectual human being: its existence is no longer confined to separate bodily parts and attachments.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00468

As the light that forms the soul grows stronger, the soul unites with the universal human spirit, called the Spirit of Holiness and the Active Intellect. This source is wide enough to include all human beings, just as a universal nature can be said of many individuals. But the universal nature is only a general idea of those individuals, while this source is their real foundation: it contains them and keeps them. General natures, too, are signs of real, luminous beings and sacred intellectual forms. In short, when the soul becomes intellect, its sense images become actual objects of thought and are themselves known, for everything that is actually understood is also an actual knower.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00469
VI. The Anqa, the spiritual being of the mystics, described through symbols
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00470

The Anqa is a real being to the mystics. They are as certain of its existence as they are of whiteness. It is a sacred bird, and its home is Mount Qaf. Its whistle wakes those asleep in the beds of darkness. Its call stirs those who have forgotten God's signs, though few listen closely or recognize its echo. Many have shut themselves off from hearing and turned away from their Lord's signs. They are deaf, mute, and blind, so they do not understand. The Anqa is with all creation, though creation is not with it. As the Persian poet says:
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00471
You are with us, yet not one of us; you are beyond us, yet never apart.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00472

Anyone suffering from dropsy or an illness of black bile may drink from its shade. Those suffering from melancholy also benefit from hearing its call. Its wings and feathers have qualities that can heal many different illnesses and diseases. But there is one deadly illness it cannot heal: deep, stubborn ignorance. It can fly up and down without moving, and come and go without any change or journey. It can be near or far without distance or place. Colors appear through it, though it has no color; the same is true of tastes and smells. Whoever understands its language understands the languages of all birds and knows every truth and secret.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00473

Not an atom in the far west is without it. All things are occupied with it, while it is free of them all. Every place is full of it, yet it has no place. The sciences and crafts come from its call; pleasing melodies, remarkable songs, and instruments of music draw their principles from this sacred bird, blessed in its nature and name. The Persian poet says:
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00474
If you have never seen Solomon, how can you know the language of birds?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00475

Whoever protects themselves with one of its feathers may pass through fire without burning and cross water without drowning. Through the support of this sacred bird, all beings reach the forms of perfection suited to them, and those who travel the path reach their aims and needs.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00476
VII. Sensory happiness and misery in the afterlife, apart from true intellectual happiness and misery
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00477

Philosophers have disagreed about whether souls that know only simple ignorance, and have not taken on any intellectual form or even basic knowledge, continue to exist after death. Alexander of Aphrodisias, one of the greatest students of Aristotle, is said to have believed that such souls perish. Avicenna also leaned toward this view in some of his writings. We have already explained that if the next life consisted only of intellectual existence, these simple souls would have to perish, because in any realm a thing exists through its form, not through its matter. But beyond this changing, bodily life there are two lasting realms of forms: one of things understood through intellect, and another of images that can be perceived without depending on matter.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00478

Only the soul preserves these sensory images there, because their existence is awareness itself. A sensed thing exists for the soul that senses it; the soul keeps these images alive without any material body, just as the intellect, by God's permission, keeps the soul alive without a bearer or body. The things of this world need only their active causes and the ends they serve; they do not need the material causes and bodily powers that prepare them here. So the soul remains after the body. If it has not acquired bodily habits or harmful traits that conflict with its original, luminous nature, it will not be tormented by them. Nor can it be left inactive, since nothing in existence is entirely inactive. Its share of pleasure and happiness is proportionate to its share of existence.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00479

As we have seen, existence brings pleasure, and fuller existence brings greater pleasure. Because this soul does not depend on matter, it exists in its own right, not merely as a feature of something else. Its pleasure therefore depends on its existence and on what is present to it, so long as nothing blocks or disturbs it. But its pleasure is weak because it has not reached its full development. It has moved beyond mere potential by learning basic truths and widely accepted ideas, yet it has not developed a settled desire for intellectual realities or a firm longing for intellectual completion. If such a soul was good, then after leaving this body it may have a kind of happiness, though not the highest kind. It may experience the images it once imagined and longed for: companions in paradise, palaces, thornless lote trees, clustered fruit, spreading shade, trees and rivers, and all the other things it heard described in religious teachings. This presents no difficulty for us, because afterlife images do not need a material subject to exist. We will explain this through careful reasoning later.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00480

The philosophers, however, report a view from Avicenna's Healing that he considers possible and cautiously stated. He says that when these souls leave their bodies, they may still be bodily in their nature and have no interest in anything beyond bodies. This keeps their attention on bodily things. Their nature may still make them long to be connected to some kind of body, though not to a human or animal body, for reasons he gives. Such a body would have matter and form, but would not be a human body. It might be a celestial body. The soul would not become the soul or ruler of that body; it would only use it to form images, since the body's matter could support imagination. The soul could then imagine the things it had believed in while alive. If it believed that goodness and good actions bring happiness, it would see beautiful things and imagine that it had died and been buried, along with all the other things its faith taught about the reward of the good.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00481

Avicenna also allows that this body could be made from air and smoke, joined to the subtle bodily spirit that natural philosophers say carries the soul's influence through the body, especially in the heart, brain, liver, arteries, nerves, and veins. If this spirit could remain intact after separating from the body and its fluids, Avicenna says, the soul might stay with it in a lasting bond. The opposite would happen to evil souls: they would imagine the punishments described in their teachings. Their happiness or misery would depend on bodies because imagination and inner judgment use bodily powers. Each group would become happier or more miserable through contact with similar souls. The truly happy would enjoy one another's company and understand themselves and those joined to them. Their connection would not be like the crowding of bodies, where space runs out. It would be a meeting of one intellect with another, which grows more spacious as more join it.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00482

This is as far as Avicenna and those like him reached in explaining sensory happiness and misery after death, and the paradise of the happy and the fire of the miserable. We have already shown, in the third chapter of the eighth book on the soul, how weak this view is and how many problems it creates. Here is one of them: how could anyone trained in natural philosophy—let alone divine philosophy—think that, once separated from this body, the soul might imagine through a body made of air and smoke? A smoky body made from the elements would scatter and dissolve at the slightest cause unless something kept it together and continually replaced what it lost, as the body's vital spirit does. If it remained prepared for the soul's use in this way, it would itself be a kind of plant or animal, since it would be the seat of imagination.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00483

Would this not be transmigration? The smoky body would be an animal other than a human, and a human soul would enter it, leaving its human nature for another animal form. To be human, a being must have the power to understand intellectual truths, either already or at least as a real possibility. But this smoky body would have no such power: death has ended its earlier possibility without making it an actual intellect. If it did regain the power to understand, it would be another human being. So how could transmigration be avoided? Avicenna and the philosophers who follow him already reject it. They cannot avoid the problem merely by saying that the soul uses this body without becoming its soul. A soul is a knowing substance that uses a living animal body as the subject of its perceptions—especially according to their own view that sensory and imagined forms exist in the bodily organs that serve them.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00484

This is a mistaken view. It was forced on them because they did not know that the imaginative soul and its images are free from natural matter. It is also surprising that Avicenna says that truly happy souls enjoy an intellectual union with one another, like one understood thing joined to another, even though he did not understand this kind of union and denied the unity of the knower and what is known throughout most of his writings. He strongly criticized Porphyry and those who followed him for defending it.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00485

At the end of The Healing and in The Adhawiyya, Avicenna writes that imagined forms are no weaker than sensory ones. In fact, they may have greater effect and clarity, as we see in dreams. What we dream may even be more important than things we sense while awake. Images in the afterlife will be more stable than dream images because there will be fewer obstacles, and the soul and the capacity receiving them will be clearer. The forms we see in dreams and while awake are all images within the soul. The difference is that dream images begin within us and descend into the outer sense, while waking images begin outside and rise inward.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00486

The image that appears in the soul is what truly gives pleasure or pain, not the thing outside it. Whatever takes form in the soul has an effect, even without an outside cause. The image within us is the direct cause; the outside thing is only an indirect cause, or a cause of that cause. So the soul feels pain or pleasure only through the image that appears within it. A beautiful sight that remains only in matter and does not enter the soul does not bring us pleasure.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00487

This is as far as the ideas of the Muslim philosophers—Avicenna, al-Farabi, and those of their time and their followers—have gone. Their account falls short of a sound investigation. It does not reach a useful conclusion, and, as we have already shown, it is false in itself. We will return to the heart of the matter when we examine the afterlife of souls that have not reached perfection or the rank of the highest beings.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00488

It is striking that the account Avicenna presents, which he attributes to the scholar Abu Nasr al-Farabi, as al-Tusi explains in his commentary on Pointers and Reminders, is better than the accounts found in other Muslim writings. Al-Ghazali chose it in many of his works, as passages in The Revival of the Religious Sciences and elsewhere show. In his well-known treatise The Work Kept Hidden, he says that we should believe in the promised bodily pleasures of paradise, such as eating and sexual pleasure, because they are possible. As we have said, pleasures are sensory, imaginal, or intellectual. Sensory pleasure is clear enough, and it is just as possible in the next life as it is in this one, once the soul is returned to the body; we have already shown this by proof.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00489

Imaginal pleasure is like the pleasure of a dream, except that dreams do not last. If they did, we would not be able to tell imaginal pleasure from sensory pleasure. We take pleasure in an image because it is present to our imagination and senses, not simply because it exists outside us. If something existed outside us but left no impression on our senses, it would bring us no pleasure. And if the image remained in us after the outside thing had disappeared, the pleasure would continue.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00490

The imaginative power can invent images in this world. But an invented image is not something we can see with our eyes. If we imagine a beautiful person in perfect detail and picture them standing before us, we do not feel great joy, because we cannot actually see them as we can in a dream. If imagination could place the image before our sight as it places it within itself, our pleasure would be much greater. The image would then be like something really present. In the next life, the power to present an image to the sight is complete. Whatever a person longs for appears before them in the imagination and is seen.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00491

This is what the Prophet's saying points to: “There is a market in paradise where images are sold.” The market means God's grace, the source of our power to create images that answer our desires. This power is broader and more complete than the power to bring something into being outside the senses. It is fitting to understand the next life in the way that most fully answers our desires. The fact that its pleasures exist in our senses, rather than outside us, does not make them any less real. They exist for our enjoyment, and our share of them is fulfilled when they appear to our senses. Their existence outside us would be an extra, not something we need. In this limited world, outside things are the route to what we want; in the next world, that route is open and unrestricted.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00492

There is also a third kind of existence, the intellectual. On this level, things we perceive through the senses are images of higher realities that the senses cannot perceive. Just as there are many different kinds of things we can sense, there are many kinds of intellectual realities. Each pleasure of the senses can stand as an image of a different intellectual pleasure, and its rank among pleasures of the senses corresponds to the rank of that intellectual reality.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00493

The view of the afterlife held by theologians such as Fakhr al-Din al-Razi falls below this account. They say that resurrection means gathering scattered material parts—especially the supposedly permanent parts of the original limbs—and giving them a form like the body's former shape, so that the soul can be attached to them again. They do not see that this would be a resurrection in this world, not in a new realm; it would return us to the first home, where we work and learn, rather than the next home, where we are repaid and brought to completion. How would this avoid transmigration? What, then, is the meaning of God's words: “We are able to replace you with others like you and bring you into a form you do not know”; and “We have set death among you, and nothing can prevent Us from replacing you with others like you and bringing you into a form you do not know”; and “We created them and strengthened their bodies, and, if We will, We can replace them with others just like them”?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00494

Anyone with insight can see that the next life is another mode of existence, different from this one made of earth, water, and clay. Death and resurrection begin the soul's return to God, or its drawing near to Him, not its return to a dense, dark body made from earthly matter.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00495

In his great commentary, Fakhr al-Din al-Razi tries to prove the meaning of resurrection that he has understood from Qur'anic verses about the Day of Judgment. He interprets them in a way that suits his own view. He says that verses in the chapter The Event answer the objection of the deniers, who ask: “When we are dead and become dust and bones, will we really be raised? And our forefathers too?” The verses show that resurrection is possible in four ways.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00496

First, God says: “Have you considered the seed you emit? Do you create it, or are We its Creator?” Al-Razi's argument is this. Semen, according to the old medical account, is the finest residue of the body's final stage of digestion. It spreads through the limbs like dew, and all the limbs contribute to it. This, he says, is why ritual washing follows sexual pleasure: the body's parts have all been relieved of their contribution. God then gives desire the power to gather these scattered, dew-like parts into a bodily structure. At first they were spread across the body, even as far as its extremities.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00497

God gathers them in the animal's body and then in the vessels that hold semen. He brings them out as flowing fluid and places them in the womb. If He can gather parts that were so widely scattered and form a person from them, why should He be unable to gather them again after death?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00498

Al-Razi says this is the argument, and that it appears in several places in the Qur'an. In The Pilgrimage, God says: “O people, if you doubt the resurrection, We created you from dust,” and continues to say that God is the truth, gives life to the dead, has power over all things, and will raise those in the graves. In The Believers, after describing the stages of creation, God says: “Then after that you will die; then on the Day of Resurrection you will be raised.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00499

The same argument appears in The Resurrection: “Was he not a drop of semen emitted, then a clinging form, which God created and shaped?” And in The Night Visitor: “Let the human being consider what he was created from,” followed by the words that God can bring him back.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00500

The second argument comes from God's words: “Have you considered what you sow? Do you make it grow, or do We make it grow?” Al-Razi's reasoning is that seeds come in many shapes: split or whole, round, three-sided, square, and more. When a seed is placed in the ground and surrounded by water and soil, one might expect it to rot, since either of these would be enough to cause decay, let alone both together. Yet it remains intact. When it absorbs enough moisture, it splits in two. One part grows upward, while the other takes hold in the soil. Even a hard date stone splits in half by God's permission. One part grows upward and the other downward. Though both parts share the same nature and elements, one is light and rises while the other is heavy and sinks. This shows a complete power and wisdom beyond the reach of human understanding. How, then, could this power be unable to gather scattered parts and assemble limbs?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00501

The third argument comes from God's words: “Have you considered the water you drink? Did you send it down from the clouds, or did We send it down?” Al-Razi gives several reasons. First, water is naturally heavy, so making it rise goes against its nature. There must be a powerful agent that overcomes its natural tendency, directs it, and makes what normally falls rise. Second, the scattered particles of water come together after being dispersed. There must be an agent that gathers them, drop by drop. The One who gathers tiny droplets of water for rain can gather the scattered particles of earth for resurrection.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00502
Third, the water is moved by the winds. Fourth, it is sent down where it is needed, onto parched land. All this, Al-Razi says, points to resurrection.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00503

The fourth argument comes from God's words: “Have you considered the fire you kindle? Did you bring forth its tree, or did We bring it forth?” Al-Razi says that fire naturally rises while a tree grows downward. Fire is bright, while the tree is dark; fire is hot and dry, while the tree is cool and moist. God holds the bright parts of fire within the dark tree. By His power, He brings together things with opposite qualities. If He is able to do this, how could He be unable to assemble an animal's parts and limbs?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00504

That, then, is the furthest the theologians' understanding and the formal scholars' reasoning have gone in trying to establish the next life, the resurrection of bodies, and the raising of spirits and souls. Even setting aside the weaknesses in their argument and their distortion of the Qur'anic verses—whose meaning and purpose we will explain later—the account they give does not establish another realm or explain belief in the Day of Judgment at all.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00505

What their account establishes is only that scattered parts, spread across different places in this world, could be gathered in one place and arranged together, then given a form like the one that had disappeared. After a long period of rest in its immaterial, holy realm, the soul would return to this world and become attached once more to a dense, dark body. They call it the Day of Resurrection because the soul then stands up from its natural body, no longer needing it and existing through itself and its Creator. In the next life, the body depends on the soul; here, the soul depends on the natural body, because its existence here is weak and its existence there is strong.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00506

In short, Al-Razi's account sounds more like the words of those who deny the next life than those who affirm it. Many naturalists and materialists said much the same: the elements gather through winds, rain, and the rays of the sun and moon, producing human beings, animals, and plants. These beings die, and their forms break apart. Later, the same parts gather again in the same or a similar arrangement, producing more beings like the first—either with the same souls, as those who believe in transmigration say, or with new souls replacing the old ones.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00507

Who, I ask, has denied that the same water, earth, and matter can produce a form like the first one more than once? The point is not simply to show that God has the power to do this. The people who argue in this way, with polished words and endless disputes, have missed the purpose of religious duties, revealed laws, messengers, and scriptures. Their purpose is to complete human souls and free them from this world of opposites, from the grip of desire, and from the limits of place and direction. This completion and freedom come only when we pass from this changing, temporary life into a lasting, unchanging one.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00508

To make that passage, we must first know about the lasting realm and believe that it is real. Second, we must know that it is the true goal of human life, toward which our nature would turn if ignorance and wrongdoing did not lead us astray. Third, we must act in keeping with that goal, follow the paths that lead to it, and remove whatever blocks the way.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00509

The purpose of the Qur'anic verses that point to the truth of the afterlife is to awaken us to another mode of existence and guide us toward a world hidden from our senses and beyond the sight of creatures. This is the unseen world; our present world is the visible one. The first is the world of spirits, the second the world of bodies. Just as the spirit is hidden within the body, the next life is hidden within this one.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00510

It is difficult for most people to grasp a mode of existence unlike this natural world, or another realm hidden within the one we see. So they deny it. They are also so attached to their bodies, desires, and pleasures that they find it hard to leave them and seek a life unlike this one. They do not reflect on what the next life is or how it works. Instead, they turn away from it and from its signs. God says: “How many signs in the heavens and earth do they pass by, turning away from them?” They are content with this life, at ease in it, and cling to the earth, as God says of one who “inclined toward the earth and followed his own desire.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00511

We have seen many people associated with learning and religious law shrink from affirming a world beyond matter. Their hearts recoil at the words intellect, soul, and spirit, and at praise of that world or criticism of bodies, their passing pleasures, and their eventual end. Most imagine that the next life is like this one, only richer, longer, and more lasting. They are drawn to it and perform acts of worship for its sake, hoping to satisfy the desires of the belly and the sex. That is why the Qur'an repeatedly speaks of the next life, resurrection, and rising from the dead: to wake people from ignorance and heedlessness, turn them toward the next life, free them from the body's chains and this world's attachments, cleanse them of what stains them, and make them long to meet God, live near those brought close to Him, and join the holy ones.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00512

Know that the purpose of the verses we have cited is not to prove, as Al-Razi explains, a random power of the sort attributed to the Ash'arites—a power that denies wisdom and rejects the connection between cause and effect. The strange thing is that whenever these people try to establish a basic religious belief, such as God's power, prophecy, or resurrection, they feel forced to deny the natural powers God placed in things, to reject rational connections between them, and to deny the ordered structure of existence that follows from their natures. God's way does not change. Yet they use this approach to establish many of their beliefs, as did the leading debater and theologian Al-Razi.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00513

You may ask: What, then, do these verses mean, especially the ones that describe semen and the beginning of creation? Do they not mean that God, who can create something for the first time, can also create it again?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00514

I answer: the main purpose of these verses about resurrection is to point to two sound ways of explaining the return of souls and bodies. The first establishes it through the goal toward which things are directed and the goals built into their natures. The second establishes it through the agent that brings them about.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00515

A proof is strongest when its middle step is the cause of its conclusion—that is, when the middle step explains why the conclusion follows. This is called a demonstrative proof. A weaker argument uses a middle step that is itself an effect of the point it is trying to prove. Of all proofs that proceed through causes, the strongest are those that show either the acting cause or the final goal. We can now see this in the verses.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00516

The verses about semen and its stages describe it changing from a lower form to a higher one and from a lesser state to a fuller one. Their purpose is to show that these stages and changes have a final goal. Human beings naturally move toward completion. We have an inborn, God-given path toward the active source of life and the completion fitting for us. But that completion is not found in this lower world. It is found in the next life, where we return and reach our final end.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00517

Once a person has passed through all the natural stages of growth—matter, plant life, and animal life—and has reached bodily maturity, their worldly, animal existence is complete. They must then turn toward the next life, bringing what has not yet developed to completion, and moving from this world to the next. Their Lord is the ultimate goal, the end of every longing and movement. This is what the verse means when it says, “O people, if you doubt the resurrection, We created you from dust, then from a drop of fluid,” and continues by promising that God will raise those in the graves—the graves of bodies and the graves of spirits, meaning their bodies. The other verses that describe the stages of creation and the development of semen make the same point: human life and its natural movement have a final goal in the next life.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00518
You may ask: These stages of growth also occur in things other than human beings, such as plants and animals. Must they, too, have a next life?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00519

I answer: they pass through some, but not all, of these stages. Their nature is less complete than human nature, so their goal lies beyond the stages they have reached. An animal that has not reached the human level cannot enter the spiritual world or approach the holy realm, just as a plant cannot reach the human level without first passing through animal life. This is not transmigration from one body to another, but a different kind of passage, understood by those with insight and wisdom. And not everything that moves toward a goal is sure to reach it. Something outside it may block the way. The point is that each nature has a goal fixed by its original constitution, even though obstacles may prevent it from arriving.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00520

The verses that argue from the creation of great heavenly bodies and the kinds of nature establish the next life through the acting cause. Many people think that nothing can come into being without a material source. They deny that another realm with new forms and bodies can begin, because they assume it must be made from some existing matter. They do not understand that the beings of the next life are brought into existence through the power of an agent, not fashioned from prior matter prepared to receive them.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00521

God shows that His primary way of acting is to bring things into being directly, not to shape and assemble them from earlier matter. The heavens, the earth, and the basic kinds of beings were created in this way. They were not made from some earlier matter. In the same way, paradise, hell, and the bodies raised in the next life are brought into being. This answers those who ask what matter the next life will be made from, or in what region, place, or time it will exist. They demand a particular place in this world and ask when the Hour will come to rest, as though it must occupy some place among these bodies and some fixed time in this worldly age. They do not understand that the place and time of the next life are not the same kind as the place and time of this one. Nor does it come into being in the same way as beings in this world. Its existence is stronger, because it comes directly from God's creative act.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00522

This is a subtle and noble way of reading the verses. It is more fitting and easier for the First Cause to bring forms into being without prior matter than to assemble and combine scattered parts. Direct creation is God's special act, higher and nobler than gathering what has been scattered and joining what has been separated. Gathering and joining are the work of limited powers and natural forces, which are weaker in their ability to act.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00523

If God first brought human beings into existence by combining the elements and their mixtures, He can bring them into existence again without matter. You already know that all existence comes from Him. The intermediaries do not create; they specify and direct His act or multiply the ways His gift of existence reaches things. What is simpler and less divided is closer to the true source. We have already said that beings in the next life are purer than combinations and mixtures, and closer to perfect unity than the beings of this world.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00524

So just as God's special act in the beginning was to bring the first realm into existence, not to combine different things and gather scattered parts, the true resurrection is the direct creation of the second realm. This is easier for Him than creating beings in this world through movement and change in matter. The next life is better, more lasting, and higher; so it is more fitting to come from the Highest Source, as God says: “That is easier for Him,” and “His is the highest likeness in the heavens and earth.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00525

Know that the next life is called “next” only in relation to our own development. In itself, it is earlier and more basic, because in the order of existence it comes before the natural world in rank and nobility. It comes after the natural world only as we experience it and grow toward it. This also shows that the next life already exists, and that paradise and hell were created long ago, as many verses and reports say.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00526

Another sign that creating the beings of the next life accords more closely with God's way of direct creation is this: beings in this world come into existence and reach completion gradually. They develop over time, and the many members of each kind do not all appear at once. Some are born before others, and one generation must end before another begins. God says: “Every community has its appointed term; when its term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour or bring it forward.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00527

The forms of the next life, however, are brought into being all at once, without birth from parents or gradual development. God says: “The first and the last will surely be gathered together at the appointed time.” Their existence comes in a single act, by God's permission, when Israfil breathes their spirits into the forms of their bodies, which come from those spirits. It is one blast, and suddenly they are all there.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00528
VIII. The different views about resurrection
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00529

Among the common errors and ignorant views is the claim that neither souls nor bodies can be raised, and that resurrection is impossible. This is the view of atheists, naturalists, materialists, and some natural philosophers and doctors whose opinions carry no authority in religion or philosophy. They assume that a human being is nothing more than this visible body, its bodily balance, and the powers and qualities that depend on it. They say that all these things disappear at death, leaving only scattered matter. A human being, like any animal or plant, is gone once dead; happiness and misery are limited to bodily pleasures and pains in this worldly life. This view contradicts reason, as the careful philosophers have shown, and revelation, as the careful religious scholars have shown.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00530

Galen is reported to have hesitated over the afterlife because he was unsure what the soul is. If it is only the body's balance, he thought, it will perish at death and cannot be raised. But if it is a being in its own right that does not depend on matter, it will survive death and can be raised. Some who cling to the authority of scholars add that something once destroyed cannot be brought back, so a human being whose body has perished cannot be restored. The theologians answered this in two ways. Some denied that what has been destroyed cannot return; others denied that the human being perishes when the body's structure breaks down. They said that some parts of the human being remain, either as divisible pieces or as indivisible ones, and interpreted the scriptural accounts of resurrection as referring to the gathering of those scattered, surviving parts.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00531

To make resurrection fit their view, the theologians have accepted one of two strange and far-fetched ideas. Neither is required by reason or revelation. Both reason and revelation tell us that the person raised in the next life is the same one who acted, worked, and was bound by intellectual and religious duties.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00532

The root of the deniers' doubt will not be removed until we uproot their basic assumption: that a person is destroyed at death and nothing remains, because a human being is only a body with a certain balance or a form that inhabits it. We have already refuted that assumption at length. The leading philosophers and religious scholars agree that the next life is real and that there is a lasting realm, though they disagree about how resurrection happens.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00533

Most Muslim scholars, jurists, and traditionalists say that resurrection is bodily only. They regard the spirit as a body that flows through the limbs as fire moves through coal, water through a rose, or oil through an olive. Most philosophers, following Aristotle's school, say that resurrection is spiritual or intellectual only. They say that the body, its form, and its qualities perish when the soul's connection to it ends, so the same body cannot return. Since the soul exists in its own right without depending on matter and survives death, it returns to the realm of immaterial beings when its natural bond to the body is cut.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00534

Many of the greatest philosophers, mystics, and theologians—including al-Ghazali, al-Ka'bi, al-Halimi, al-Raghib al-Isfahani, and several leading Imami scholars—say that both kinds of resurrection take place. They hold that the immaterial soul returns to a body in the next life. Most Christians and those who believe in transmigration also affirm a soul's return to a body, but there is an important difference: the careful Muslim scholars say that souls begin to exist and are returned to bodies in the next life, while those who believe in transmigration say that souls have always existed and return to bodies in this world. They deny the next life and bodily paradise and hell.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00535

Those who affirm both kinds of resurrection also disagree about whether the body raised is this very body or only a similar one. They also ask whether sameness or similarity must apply to every limb, shape, and feature. It seems that no one requires every detail to be the same. Many Muslim scholars appear to hold that the body raised will differ from the first in its form and shape. They sometimes point to reports describing the people of paradise and hell: the people of paradise are said to be smooth-skinned and beardless, while an unbeliever's tooth is said to be as large as Mount Uhud. They also cite God's words: “Whenever their skins are burned away, We replace them with other skins, so that they may taste the punishment,” and “Is the One who created the heavens and earth not able to create others like them?”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00536
You may ask: On this account, would not the person rewarded or punished with bodily pleasures and pains be someone other than the one who performed the good or evil acts?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00537

The answer is that what matters is the one who experiences them. That is the soul, whether it experiences them directly or through bodily instruments. The soul remains the same. We say that a person from childhood to old age is the very same person, even though their form, size, shape, qualities, many bodily parts, and powers have changed. We do not say that someone who did wrong in youth and is punished in old age is being punished for another person's crime.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00538

That is how the different views are stated. The truth, as you will learn, is that the person raised in the next life is this very same person, both in soul and in body. The soul is this same soul, and the body is this same body: if you saw it, you would say, “I have seen this very person—the one who lived in this world.” This is so even though the body has undergone many changes, to the point where we might say, “This has become gold,” or “This has become iron,” and eventually both may become one, pure intellect. Whoever denies this rejects religious teaching and falls short in wisdom; they would also have to reject many clear passages of the Qur'an.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00539
IX. Arguments of those who deny resurrection
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00540

Those who deny resurrection argue, first, that something destroyed cannot be brought back. They also ask what happens if one person eats another. If the eaten person's parts are restored to the eater's body, then the eaten person has not been raised. If those parts are restored to the body they came from, then the eater has not been raised. If they are restored to both, the very same parts would be enjoying reward and suffering punishment at once, as when a believer eats an unbeliever.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00541

Theologians have answered the first objection by denying that what has been destroyed cannot return, or by denying that resurrection requires something destroyed to return. They answer the second by saying that God preserves the original parts of each person's body and does not let them become parts of another body in the same way.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00542

There have been long arguments between those who affirm resurrection and those who deny it. Repeating them would take time without bringing us closer to the truth. The theologians' arguments do not force their opponents to accept their view. How, then, can we discover the truth? Anyone who relies only on debate should first ask the deniers what they are claiming. Do they say resurrection is impossible, or only that it is not possible? If they claim impossibility, the burden is on them to prove it. They have no proof. If they only deny that it is possible, then God's revelation and the Prophet's reports—coming from one free of error and falsehood—stand in place of mathematical proof.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00543

Some thinkers have tried to explain how the body can be restored. Their argument goes like this: a person is made this particular person by the particular parts of their body and soul, not by the exact arrangement of those parts. The parts themselves remain the same, even when their arrangement breaks down at death. If those same parts are later joined again in the same general way, the original person returns. This is what one writer says.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00544

A later scholar gives a similar account. Some theologians, he says, allow that what has been destroyed can be restored, while philosophers and other theologians deny it. Yet those who affirm bodily resurrection without allowing restoration of the destroyed body do not say that bodies vanish. They say that the parts scatter and can no longer serve their former purpose. In his notes on The Guide, he says this view depends on denying that a body has a basic bodily form, and treating it instead as a collection of indivisible atoms, as theologians do. It also depends on the view that a body is a continuous shape that remains the same even when broken apart. If we accept that bodies have a basic form, he says, it is enough for bodily resurrection that the material parts be the same; the body's form may change, so long as the new form is close to the one that disappeared.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00545

If someone objects that this is transmigration, the reply is that what they reject is a soul moving into a body made of different matter. Here, the body would be made from the very same matter as before, and its form would be close to the old one. If someone calls that transmigration, the disagreement is only over words. They must prove that the thing itself is impossible.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00546
The accounts of these two respected scholars are badly reasoned, though they come closer to the truth than the accounts of other theologians. There are several problems with them.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00547

First, they assume that when a person named Zayd dies, only the relations among the body's parts and the arrangement of its limbs disappear. That would make life a kind of relation, which is plainly false.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00548

Second, even if Zayd's body were made only of indivisible atoms, it would not follow that any arrangement of those atoms would be Zayd. If any arrangement were enough, then a solid ball made from those atoms would be Zayd. If only one special arrangement counted, then a dead person would sometimes become alive whenever their parts happened to fall back into that arrangement. The scholar al-Tusi, and other reasonable thinkers who deny a separate underlying matter, did not say that an individual body survives when its parts are scattered. What they say remains is matter in general, the kind of thing that continues through joining and separation—not a particular body like this one. A body as a general kind cannot exist on its own in the world. It exists only through a form that gives it a particular nature.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00549

A human being is not simply a body. If being human meant only having a body, then every body would be human. Nor is Zayd simply a certain amount of matter. If it were, then scattered parts of his body, spread to opposite ends of the world, would still be Zayd. No reasonable person would say that a particular horse remains that very horse after it is cut into pieces and its parts are scattered.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00550

Third, the problem of transmigration clearly remains. The same body would have two souls. If the scattered parts could still receive the soul while they were separated, then the soul would never have left them; Zayd would still be alive at death, which contradicts what we assumed. If they could no longer receive a soul, they would need something new to prepare them. Once that new condition made them ready, a new soul would have to come from the Giver of life. If the returning soul then joined the parts as well, one body would have two souls, which is impossible.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00551

What special link could remain between the soul and a few scattered pieces of earth, rather than any other parts of matter? Even a weak link must arise because the two are especially suited to one another. We often see matter with a balance close to that of an animal, and so ready to receive an animal's form. It is more fit for a soul than gray, scattered parts that are no longer suited even to a lifeless form, let alone to plant life, animal life, or human life—and still less to being Zayd.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00552

Anyone who looks within knows that a soul is not drawn to one body or some of its parts rather than others unless those parts have a quality or shape that fits it. Tell me, thoughtful reader: what bond could the soul have with parts scattered in the air, buried in the ground, or lost in water, when neither sight nor imagination can distinguish them from other parts? Even if God knows them as different, that difference creates no special link. Nor, according to these thinkers, does the soul remember the body after its powers break down, so memory cannot single out the parts of its former body. And even if memory did remain and could identify that body, it would explain only why this soul returned to this body rather than another. It would not explain why this same soul, rather than another soul, returned to it.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00553

These problems and far-fetched explanations disappear only through the truth we have established. God has given us this share of the higher wisdom, along with other rare insights. Anyone who follows God's path and receives the light of divine knowledge can recognize its truth and worth, just as a skilled jeweler can tell a bright gem from other stones.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00554
X. How people differ in their understanding of the afterlife
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00555
Know that people who believe in the truth of resurrection and the raising of bodies hold different views, each suited to a different level of understanding.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00556

The first and lowest level is the ordinary Muslim's belief. It is the simplest view and the least open to harmful doubts: everything described about the next life—the punishment in the grave, its pressure, the questioning by Munkar and Nakir, snakes, scorpions, and more—really happens as something physical that the eye could see. God simply does not allow people to see it while they are alive, for a wise purpose. Some verses and reports appear to support this view.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00557

The second view is that the promised rewards and punishments are like what we see in dreams. They are imaginal forms, with no material existence outside the soul, just like the snakes and scorpions a person sees in a dream. Yet a dream can cause real pain. The sleeper may cry out, sweat, and toss about. Dreams can also bring intense pleasure, sometimes greater than anything felt while awake. The sleeper sees forms, acts, and responds, while the body lies still. No snake is actually nearby, yet for the sleeper the snake and its bite are real. If the pain comes from the bite, it makes no difference whether the snake is in a dream or before the eyes.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00558

The same is true of the gardens, trees, rivers, pleasant places, and gracious people we may see in a dream. They are real for the sleeper as objects of inner awareness, even though they do not exist outside or appear to the waking senses. Avicenna leaned toward this view when he discussed the paradise of people whose knowledge is incomplete and the fire of those whose actions fall short. Al-Ghazali followed him, as we have seen.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00559
The third view accepts the images promised for the Day of Resurrection, but understands them in one of two ways.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00560

The first is that the forms perceived through the senses and described in religious teaching point to separate intellectual forms in the world of pure intellect. Plato and his followers held that every kind of thing perceived through the senses has a corresponding intellectual form, or pattern, in that world. Seeing the next life in this intellectual way is possible only for people of deep knowledge and complete understanding. It is not for those with simple minds or still, undeveloped souls, who make up most of the people in paradise. A report says that most of its people are simple folk.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00561

Al-Ghazali says in one of his treatises that all these views are possible. A person may receive what suits their readiness. Someone whose love of religious teaching has made them deeply attached to its outward forms will not find a path to the deeper truths, or see the intellectual forms. Those who know the truth and look down on bodily images and pleasures will receive subtle joys and intellectual pleasures suited to them. These will satisfy their longing. Paradise gives each person what they desire. Desires differ, so gifts and pleasures may also differ. God's power is vast; human beings cannot take in all its wonders. Through the prophets, God has made known as much of it as people can understand. We must believe what they understand, and accept that there are other matters beyond the reach of our knowledge.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00562

The second way to understand these promised images is that they stand for the kinds of joy or pain that follow from them. Al-Ghazali explains this by comparing them to dreams. If someone dreams of green fields, flowing water, a beautiful face, rivers, rain falling as milk, honey, or wine, trees decorated with jewels and pearls, palaces of gold and silver, or attendants waiting to serve, a dream interpreter would explain the dream as a kind of joy. They would not take it as a literal report about another kind of joy. Some joys come from knowledge and discovery; others come from power or from seeing friends. They may all be called pleasure, but they differ in rank and quality. We should understand intellectual pleasures in the same way, even when no eye has seen them, no ear has heard them, and no heart has imagined them.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00563

Al-Ghazali then explains how the promised images may stand for intellectual pleasure and pain. A snake itself does not hurt you; its poison does. The poison itself is not the pain either. You suffer from the effect the poison produces in you. If the same effect came about without poison, you would still suffer. We can describe this kind of pain only by linking it to the usual cause. In the same way, if a person felt sexual pleasure without the familiar act, we could describe it only by comparing it to that act. The effect is present even if its usual cause is not. A cause exists for the sake of its result, not for itself.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00564

At death, destructive traits turn into things that hurt the soul. Their pain is like a snakebite even when there are no snakes or scorpions. A quality can turn from something pleasing into something painful, just as love becomes painful when the beloved dies. What once brought joy can become such a source of suffering that the lover wishes they had never known love or union. This itself is one kind of torment after death.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00565

The fourth level is held by people firmly grounded in knowledge, who join direct experience with proof. They know with certainty that the forms described and promised in religious teaching really exist. They are real and stable. In existence, strength, permanence, and effect, they surpass the forms of this world so greatly that there is no comparison.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00566

These forms have different levels. Some are intellectual forms: the paradise of those who know God's oneness and are close to Him. Some are pleasurable sensory forms: the paradise of the people of the right, the safe, and the faithful. Others are painful forms: the hell of those who turn away, go astray, or deny the Day of Judgment. But these things are not sensed with the failing eyes and bodily senses of this world, as some literal-minded Muslims believe.
